notes.summary:
Instructional designers (IDs) spend their workday balancing creative course development with administrative and collaborative tasks. While specific daily routines vary by organization (corporate, higher education, or freelance), the role is consistently characterized by high levels of multitasking and reliance on specific software ecosystems.

### **How Instructional Designers Spend Their Time**
Instructional designers typically divide their time across five core areas. While "Development" is often the most time-consuming phase, administrative and collaborative work—such as managing SME (Subject Matter Expert) feedback and email—acts as a constant, often fragmenting, influence on their workflow.

*   **Development & Implementation (37.7%):** This is the "heavy lift," involving authoring content, building interactions, creating visuals, and recording/editing audio or video.
*   **Design (23.1%):** This stage includes writing learning objectives, creating storyboards, and mapping out the content architecture.
*   **Analysis (17.7%):** Conducting needs analysis, audience profiling, and stakeholder alignment.
*   **Admin & Project Management (12.5%):** Managing timelines, troubleshooting technical issues, and coordinating with stakeholders.
*   **Evaluation (10.6%):** Assessing course effectiveness and gathering feedback.

### **Common Tools Used on Mac**
Because many industry-standard authoring tools were originally built for Windows, Mac-based instructional designers often rely on a mix of native applications and cloud-based platforms to maintain their workflow.

*   **eLearning Authoring:** While **Articulate Storyline 360** is the industry standard, it requires a Windows environment (often via virtualization software like Parallels). Native Mac alternatives include **ActivePresenter** (all-in-one suite) and web-based tools like **Rise 360**, **Elucidat**, or **Easygenerator**.
*   **Video & Multimedia:** **Camtasia** and **ScreenFlow** (Mac-native) are highly popular for screen recording and editing. **Descript** is frequently used for text-based audio/video editing.
*   **Design & Prototyping:** **Canva** is widely used for rapid graphic design, while advanced designers may use **Adobe XD** or **Photoshop** for mockups.
*   **Collaboration & Management:** **Slack**, **Microsoft Teams**, and **Monday.com** are standard for managing communication and project status.

### **Documentation, Email, and Admin Load**
Instructional designers often face a "fragmented" workday. They frequently juggle 2–4 projects simultaneously, meaning their time is often interrupted by email and stakeholder communication. While specific data for IDs alone is limited, broader professional studies indicate that the average worker receives 126 emails per day and spends 2.6 hours on email management—a significant drain on the "deep work" required for complex course design.

### **Key Statistics**
| Statistic | Context | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **37.7%** | Time spent on development and implementation tasks. | *Synthesia/Phil.com (2024)* |
| **12.5%** | Time spent on administrative and project management tasks. | *Synthesia/Phil.com (2024)* |
| **2.6 hours** | Average time spent on email per day across professional roles. | *Agiled.app (citing Adobe/McKinsey)* |
| **38%** | Percentage of IDs who turn down work due to capacity constraints. | *Synthesia/Phil.com (2024)* |

***

### **Caveats**
*   **Calendar vs. Production Time:** It is important to distinguish between "active labor" (the hours spent building a course) and "calendar time" (the weeks or months a project takes due to waiting for SME feedback or stakeholder approval). ATD research notes that while AI has accelerated production, review cycles remain the primary bottleneck for project completion.
*   **Tooling Disagreement:** While Articulate 360 is widely cited as the most in-demand technical skill, designers working exclusively on Mac often express frustration with the lack of native, high-end authoring tools compared to their Windows counterparts.
